newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat closes lower on sharp drop in soybeans.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat closes lower on sharp drop in soybeans.

text.p: A sharp break in the soybean market, triggered by signs the U.S. may be importing soybeans from Brazil, pressed CBOT wheat futures to a lower close, traders said.
Selling was broad-based in late dealings amid the aggressive selloff in soybeans and the near limit losses in the corn pit, they said.
Wheat was higher most of the session on talk Egypt was seeking 500,000 tonnes of wheat and on ideas that U.S. soft red winter wheat acreage could be reduced, the traders said.
There were reports Egypt was seeking 500,000 tonnes wheat.
The wheat was said to be needed for May shipment but Australia was expected to contend for the business.
Talk of a cut in U.S. wheat acreage was widespread amid the recent strong rallies in soybean prices which could lead producers to plow up wheat fields and sow soy.
Also, there remains talk that some wheat acres were destroyed by the floods in the U.S. Ohio River Valley. But agronomists have said there were not very many acres of SRW in the flooded areas.
Wheat closed 2-1/2 to five cents per bushel lower, with March down five at $3.76.
"We did see a lot of people buying wheat and selling beans, getting out of those positions," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International. "Wheat showed today it is a pretender."
Traders said the late break in wheat obviously was tied to the tumble in soybeans and corn. Independently, the wheat market in early dealings found favor on several fronts.
"There was talk about plowing up SRW acres and planting beans," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "Also there's talk about full funding of EEP for 1998 beginning October 1."
Traders also said the presence of fund buying was evident in wheat and that pattern started to surface near the close of trading on Tuesday.
"Funds bought on the open and Continental was bidding then the locals ran it," a trader said. "I don't think Continental bought any but we hit stops on the open and took out some shorts."

On the day, Smith Barney bought seven million bushels of July, Refco Inc bought 3.5 million bushels of July and at least four other funds each bought two million bushels of July, traders said. Term Commodities sold six million bushels of July and FIMAT Futures sold 3.5 million bushels of July.

Technicians early Wednesday cited first resistance in the March at $3.84-1/2 and second resistance at $3.95-1/2. The session high for March was $3.83. First support was at $3.73-1/2 and second support, $3.62-1/2. The session low was $3.76.

The four and 20-day moving averages were giving off bullish signals early Tuesday. The nine day relative strength index (RSI) in the March closed at 58 percent. The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 23,000 contracts, above the 15,212 traded Tuesday.

In wheat options, Prudential Securities bought 900 July $3.50 puts and sold 900 July $3.40 puts, Term Commodities bought 400 May $3.70 puts at 5-1/2 to six cents and Continental Grain sold 400 May $3.90 calls at 11-11-1/2 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 7,000 contracts, above the 3,857 traded Tuesday.
